# How bacteria are built and get energy

> *A bacterium has to solve the same problems as one of your cells: keep its insides in, make ATP,
> and grow. This chapter asks the first two of the book's six questions of bacteria. **What is it
> built from? How does it get energy, and what does it need to grow?** The answers turn out to
> explain a great deal: why a stain turns some bacteria purple, why some die in air, and why a few
> can survive boiling.*

## Bacteria at a glance {#sec-glance}

Before you read on, try two questions. Guess if you are not sure; a wrong guess followed by the
answer is still useful.

<div data-island="quiz" data-src="/quizzes/bacteria-warmup.quiz.yml"></div>

A bacterium is a **prokaryote**: a cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. It is
also small. A typical bacterium is 1–2 µm long, about the size of a single mitochondrion, while
a human cell is usually 10–30 µm across. Almost everything else follows from building a whole,
free-living cell at that size and with that simple a plan.

The table compares a bacterium with the cells you have just studied. The last column matters for
the sixth question, *what does it have that my cells lack?* Every difference is a potential way to
harm the microbe without harming you, which is the idea the pharmacology block builds on.

| Feature | Your cells | A bacterium | Why the difference matters later |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | Yes, DNA inside a nuclear envelope | No; one circular chromosome lies free in the cytoplasm | Transcription and translation happen together |
| Mitochondria | Yes; the electron transport chain is in the inner mitochondrial membrane | None; the electron transport chain is in the cell membrane | Bacterial respiration is reachable at the cell surface |
| Ribosomes | 80S | 70S, smaller and built differently | A target that human ribosomes do not share |
| Cell wall | None | Usually a peptidoglycan wall outside the membrane | A structure with no human equivalent |
| Extra DNA | Mitochondrial DNA only | Often small circles called plasmids | Plasmids carry and share genes (the genetics chapter) |

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "bacteria have mitochondria"
Students starting microbiology often credit prokaryotes with mitochondria
[@briggs2017misconceptions]. It is an easy slip, because bacteria do respire. But they do it on
their own cell membrane. The likeness runs the other way: mitochondria are descended from bacteria
that came to live inside an ancestral cell, which is why mitochondria have their own circular DNA
and 70S-like ribosomes.
:::

## The envelope: what the cell is wrapped in {#sec-envelope}

**A bacterium's envelope is its interface with everything else**, including you. It holds the cell
together, controls what gets in and out, and carries most of what your immune system recognises.

The inside of a bacterium is full of dissolved molecules, so water tends to rush in. Without
support, the membrane would swell and burst. The support comes from **peptidoglycan**, a mesh of
sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides that wraps the whole cell like a string bag
[@silhavy2010envelope]. Human cells make nothing like it.

Most bacteria build their envelope in one of two ways:

- **Gram-positive:** a **thick peptidoglycan wall**, many layers deep, directly outside the cell
  membrane. There is no outer membrane.
- **Gram-negative:** a **thin peptidoglycan layer**, then a second, **outer membrane**. The outer
  face of that membrane is made of **lipopolysaccharide (LPS)**.

The Gram stain, developed in 1884, reads this difference in a few minutes. It still sorts most
bacteria in the lab today. Step through it, and predict the key step before you see it.

<div data-island="gram-stain" data-src="/diagrams/gram-stain.yml"></div>

**Why the envelope matters beyond the slide.** Three consequences recur through the rest of the
book.

1. **LPS is a powerful alarm signal.** Its lipid part, lipid A, is recognised by immune receptors
   and drives strong inflammation: the fever, vessel dilation and leakiness you met in general
   pathology [@raetz2002lps]. This is why LPS is also called **endotoxin**. The immunology block
   explains the receptors.
2. **The outer membrane is a barrier.** It keeps out many molecules that would reach a
   Gram-positive cell's membrane easily, including some drugs.
3. **Peptidoglycan has no human equivalent.** Anything that blocks its construction harms
   bacteria and spares you.

**Bacteria that do not fit the two designs.** *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* has a wall packed with
waxy **mycolic acids**. Gram's dyes barely penetrate it, so mycobacteria are detected with a
different method, the **acid-fast stain**. At the other extreme, *Mycoplasma* has **no wall at
all**, so it does not show up on a Gram stain, and anything aimed at the wall has nothing to act
on.

## Shape and arrangement {#sec-shape}

Bacteria come in three basic shapes: **cocci** (spheres), **bacilli** or rods, and **curved or
spiral** forms. Some also stay stuck together after dividing, in pairs, chains or clusters.

Shape and arrangement are worth knowing for one reason: **they are clues about how the cell is
built and how it divides**. They are not facts to memorise for their own sake. The activity below
puts two similar organisms side by side. Find what separates them before the explanation appears.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-staph-strep.yml"></div>

## Extra equipment: capsules, appendages, biofilms and spores {#sec-extras}

Beyond the envelope, many bacteria carry optional equipment. Each item solves a problem for the
bacterium, and each solution has a consequence for the host.

| Structure | What it is | What it does for the bacterium | Why it matters to the host |
|---|---|---|---|
| Capsule | A slimy outer layer, usually polysaccharide | Hides the cell surface; resists drying | Harder for phagocytes to grab and engulf (the host–microbe chapter) |
| Pili (fimbriae) | Short, hair-like protein fibres | Stick the cell to surfaces, including host cells | Attachment is often the first step of colonisation |
| Flagella | Long, rotating protein tails | Swimming towards nutrients | Lets bacteria move into new places |
| Biofilm | A community of cells in a shared slime matrix | Shelter from drying, predators and chemicals | Forms on teeth and on medical devices such as catheters |
| Endospore | A dormant, dehydrated cell with tough protective coats | Survives starvation, heat and chemicals for years | Hard to kill with routine heat or disinfectant |

Spores are made by a few groups of **Gram-positive rods**, notably *Bacillus* and *Clostridium*.
When food runs out, the cell builds a spore inside itself: a copy of its DNA wrapped in a
dehydrated core and several protective coats [@setlow2014spores]. When conditions improve, the
spore germinates back into a growing cell.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Predict: will boiling or an alcohol hand rub kill spores? (Click to check)
**Mostly not.** Many spores survive boiling at 100 °C, and alcohol hand rubs do not kill them
[@setlow2014spores]. Reliable killing needs pressurised steam at 121 °C, as in an autoclave. This
is one reason some hospital wards ask staff to wash hands with soap and water: the friction and
rinsing physically remove spores that alcohol would leave behind. The detecting and controlling
chapter returns to this.
:::

## Getting energy {#sec-energy}

**Bacteria make ATP with the same chemistry as your cells**, just with more variety. Your cells
break down glucose by **glycolysis**, then pass electrons down the electron transport chain to
oxygen. Bacteria use those same two stages, with one important freedom: oxygen is not the only
possible end point.

| Strategy | What happens | Final electron acceptor | ATP per glucose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aerobic respiration | Glycolysis, then an electron transport chain in the cell membrane | Oxygen | High (similar to your cells) |
| Anaerobic respiration | The same, but without oxygen | Another molecule, such as nitrate or sulfate | Lower |
| Fermentation | Glycolysis only; pyruvate is converted to products such as lactate or alcohol | None; no electron transport chain | Low (about 2) |

::: {.callout-note}
## Bridge from cell biology
Fermentation is not exotic. Your own muscle cells do it during a sprint, turning pyruvate into
lactate when oxygen supply cannot keep up. Some bacteria live this way all the time.
:::

## The oxygen spectrum {#sec-oxygen}

Oxygen is the best electron acceptor available, but it is also chemically dangerous. Partly used
oxygen forms **reactive oxygen species**, such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, which damage
proteins and DNA. You met these as by-products of your own mitochondria.

So every bacterium has to settle two questions. **Can it use oxygen to make ATP? Does oxygen harm
it?** The answers place it in one of five groups.

| Group | Uses oxygen to make ATP? | Harmed by normal air? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Obligate aerobe | Yes, and has no alternative | No | *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* |
| Facultative anaerobe | Yes, when oxygen is present; ferments otherwise | No | *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus* |
| Microaerophile | Yes, but only at low oxygen levels | Yes, at full air levels | *Campylobacter jejuni* |
| Aerotolerant anaerobe | No; ferments only | No; it has protective enzymes | Streptococci, *Lactobacillus* |
| Obligate anaerobe | No | Yes | *Bacteroides fragilis*, *Clostridium* species |

You do not need to memorise that table. If you know how an organism handles energy and oxygen,
you can work out where it will grow. Try it: the organisms below are described only by their
metabolism, and their names appear after you choose.

<div data-island="oxygen-tube" data-src="/diagrams/oxygen-tube.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "anaerobes die because they lack catalase and superoxide dismutase"
Older textbooks explain oxygen toxicity this way. The explanation came from a 1970s observation
that was later over-read. Many anaerobes do carry these protective enzymes; *Bacteroides
fragilis*, for example, makes both. What oxygen damages is the machinery anaerobes depend on:
central enzymes built around exposed iron–sulfur clusters or radical chemistry, which oxygen and
reactive oxygen species inactivate directly [@lu2021anaerobes]. An obligate anaerobe is not
defenceless. It has built its metabolism from parts that oxygen breaks.
:::

**Why this matters in the body.** Your body has oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor places. Skin and
airways are exposed to air. The colon is almost free of oxygen, and anaerobes there outnumber
facultative bacteria many times over. The body carries roughly 4 × 10^13^ bacteria, almost all
of them in the colon [@sender2016cells]. Oxygen-poor niches also appear when tissue loses its blood supply. Dead
(necrotic) tissue and the centre of an abscess, both from general pathology, have little oxygen,
so they suit anaerobes.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-ecoli-bacteroides.yml"></div>

## Growth: how bacteria multiply {#sec-growth}

Bacteria reproduce by **binary fission**: the cell copies its chromosome, grows, and splits in
two. The time this takes is the **doubling time**. In ideal laboratory conditions, *E. coli*
doubles about every 20 minutes; *M. tuberculosis* takes most of a day.

Doubling adds up fast. Starting from $N_0$ cells, after time $t$ with doubling time $g$:

$$ N = N_0 \times 2^{t/g} $$

One *E. coli* cell doubling every 20 minutes becomes about 17 million cells in 8 hours (24
doublings). A slow doubler like *M. tuberculosis* takes weeks to form a visible colony, so its
culture takes weeks too.

In a closed container, growth follows four phases:

1. **Lag:** cells adjust to new conditions; little division.
2. **Exponential (log):** steady doubling, as in the equation above.
3. **Stationary:** nutrients run low and waste builds up; division and death balance.
4. **Death:** more cells die than divide.

Rapidly dividing cells are the most vulnerable to many antimicrobial drugs, a point the
pharmacology block returns to.

## Putting it together: two microbe profiles {#sec-profiles}

Every organism in this book gets the same five-slot card: **identity and structure**, **lifestyle
and niche**, **mechanism of harm**, **general consequence** and a **contrast partner** it is
easily confused with. The organ-system blocks will later add where it infects, how it is
diagnosed and how it is treated. The card gives those facts somewhere to go.

The first card has three slots filled in; predict the other two. The second has only one filled
in.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/profile-s-aureus.yml"></div>

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/profile-b-fragilis.yml"></div>

Notice what the two cards share. Both organisms live harmlessly on or in many healthy people
[@kluytmans1997carriage], and both cause harm mainly when they reach a place they do not belong.
Both tend to produce pus and abscesses, and the capsule of *B. fragilis* actively promotes abscess
formation [@tzianabos1993abscess]. The differences come straight from this chapter's two
questions: one envelope design or the other, oxygen-tolerant or not.

## The two questions, answered {#sec-close}

This chapter built a **trait toolkit** for bacteria. Later chapters reuse it for every organism
you meet.

| Trait | The options | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Envelope | Gram-positive · Gram-negative · acid-fast (waxy) · no wall | What the immune system sees (LPS or not); what can get in; whether wall-targeting drugs can act |
| Shape and arrangement | Cocci · rods · curved or spiral; clusters · chains · pairs | Clues to identity and to how the cell divides |
| Extra equipment | Capsule · pili · flagella · biofilm · spores | How it sticks, moves, hides and survives outside a host |
| Energy and oxygen | Aerobe · facultative · microaerophile · aerotolerant · anaerobe | Where in the body it can live; how a sample must be handled |
| Growth rate | Doubling in minutes or in a day | How fast an infection develops; how long culture takes |

The next questions, *how does it copy itself and change?*, belong to the genetics chapter. *How
does damage happen?* gets its full answer in the host–microbe chapter.
